etymology: The fourth chapter of Paul’s epistle to the Ephesians; the hinge from the doctrine of chapters 1–3 to the walk of chapters 4–6.
biblical_def: Ephesians 4 is the great turning of Paul’s epistle from doctrine to duty, where the apostle, having set forth the riches of grace and the eternal purpose of God in the first three chapters, beseeches the saints to walk worthy of the calling wherewith they are called. The chapter opens with the unity of the Spirit, grounded in seven ones—one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all—a unity the church does not create but keeps in the bond of peace. Then the ascended Christ is shown giving gifts to His church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, given for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the edifying of the body, that the church may grow up into the Head, into Christ, no more tossed about by every wind of doctrine. The chapter closes with the new walk: putting off the old man, corrupt according to the deceitful lusts, and putting on the new man, created after God in righteousness and true holiness—speaking truth, laboring honestly, grieving not the Holy Spirit, and forgiving as God in Christ has forgiven. The dictionary reads Ephesians 4 as the pattern of the church’s unity, ministry, and sanctification: doctrine first, then the walk that flows from it.
webster_summary: The fourth chapter of Ephesians; the unity of the Spirit, the ascended Christ’s gifts to His church, and the putting off of the old man and putting on of the new.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the chapter’s gifts are misread to support continuing apostles, and its unity is invoked to flatten doctrinal difference.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two misreadings touch the chapter. The first takes the gift of apostles and prophets as offices continuing in the church today, the proof-text of the New Apostolic Reformation; but the apostles and prophets are named the foundation of the church (Eph 2:20), and a foundation is laid once—the dictionary holds the cessation of these founding offices with the close of the canon. The second invokes the unity of the Spirit to flatten real doctrinal difference, as though peace were purchased by silence on the truth; but the same chapter sets the goal as growing up into the Head and no more being tossed by every wind of doctrine. True unity is unity in the truth.

The principle to recover is the chapter’s own order: the unity the church keeps is grounded in the seven ones and aims at maturity in sound doctrine; the gifts are given to edify the body until it grows up into Christ; and the new walk flows from the new man created in righteousness and true holiness. Doctrine produces duty; the worthy walk is the fruit of the grace set forth in the chapters before.

etymology: The thirtieth chapter of Proverbs, the words of Agur the son of Jakeh; one of the appended collections of the book of wisdom.
biblical_def: Proverbs 30 is the chapter of Agur the son of Jakeh, a humble and remarkable section of the book of wisdom that opens not with a boast of knowledge but with a confession of ignorance: surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man, neither learned wisdom nor have the knowledge of the holy. From this lowliness Agur ascends to the unsearchable greatness of God—who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? what is his name, and what is his son’s name, if thou canst tell? He then sets the purity and sufficiency of God’s Word as a shield to them that trust in Him, with the solemn warning to add not unto His words. The chapter contains the famous prayer of contentment—give me neither poverty nor riches, feed me with food convenient for me—lest fullness breed denial of God or want drive to theft and the profaning of His name. It closes with the numerical sayings, the things that are never satisfied, the four things little upon the earth but exceeding wise, and the dignified things in their going. The dictionary reads Proverbs 30 as a school of humility before the unsearchable God, the sufficiency of His pure Word, and the wisdom of contentment.
webster_summary: The thirtieth chapter of Proverbs, the words of Agur; humility before the unsearchable God, the purity and sufficiency of His Word, and the prayer for contentment.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though Agur’s charge to add nothing to God’s pure Word rebukes every age that would amend Scripture to suit itself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle the chapter presses against every age is the sufficiency and inviolability of God’s Word: every word of God is pure, a shield to them that trust in Him, and the man who adds to His words shall be reproved and found a liar. The perennial temptation—ancient and modern alike—is to amend Scripture to the taste of the hour, to add the traditions of men or to subtract what offends, and so to be found a liar against the God who gave it. Agur’s confession of his own brutishness is the posture of the reader who would hear God rather than correct Him.

The principle to recover is humility before the unsearchable God and contentment under His hand. Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches but for food convenient, lest abundance tempt him to deny the LORD or want drive him to dishonor His name—a prayer the prosperous and the anxious age alike need to learn. The wise man begins by confessing he has not the knowledge of the holy, and ends by trusting the pure Word of the God whose name and whose Son’s name are above his telling.

etymology: The second chapter of the epistle of James; the great passage on partiality, the royal law, and faith and works.
biblical_def: James 2 is the chapter that forbids the respect of persons in the church and shows that a living faith is known by its works. James first rebukes partiality: to honor the rich man in fine apparel and to despise the poor man in vile raiment is to become a judge of evil thoughts and to transgress the royal law, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. He then turns to the great theme—faith without works is dead. A man may say he has faith, but if it has no works, can that faith save him? Faith that does not feed the hungry or clothe the naked is dead, being alone; even the devils believe, and tremble. James points to Abraham, justified when he offered Isaac, and to Rahab, justified when she received the messengers—faith made perfect, that is, shown and proved, by works. As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also. The dictionary reads James not as contradicting Paul but as completing him: Paul declares that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, speaking of the ground of justification before God; James declares that the faith which justifies is never alone but is proved living by its fruit. The faith that saves is the faith that works.
webster_summary: The second chapter of James; the rebuke of partiality, the royal law of love, and the truth that faith without works is dead—completing, not contradicting, Paul.

Jas 2:8

corruption_summary: James 2 is misread as contradicting Paul on justification, and its “works” are claimed for a salvation by works; rightly read, it completes Paul—the faith that justifies is never alone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to answer is the old claim that James contradicts Paul, set against the Reformation’s justification by faith alone, and used to smuggle works back into the ground of salvation. But James and Paul speak to different questions. Paul declares the ground of a sinner’s acceptance before God: a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, by the imputed righteousness of Christ. James declares the proof of a living faith before men: the faith that truly justifies is never alone, but shows itself living by its works, as Abraham’s faith was proved when he offered Isaac. The justification by faith alone is a justification by a faith that is never alone.

The principle to recover is the wholeness of the Reformation doctrine: faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is a working faith. A bare profession without fruit is dead, being alone—the faith of devils, who believe and tremble. James does not add works to the ground of acceptance; he tests the reality of the faith that lays hold of Christ. The tree is known by its fruit; the faith that saves is the faith that works by love.
roots_summary: James 2; the rebuke of partiality, the royal law, and faith without works being dead; completes Paul rather than contradicting him.

etymology: The first chapter of Paul’s epistle to the Colossians; the great hymn to the supremacy of Christ.
biblical_def: Colossians 1 is the chapter of Christ’s supremacy, written to a church threatened by a philosophy that would dethrone the Son, and answering every such threat by exalting Him to His rightful place over all things. After thanksgiving and prayer that the saints might be filled with the knowledge of God’s will, Paul sets forth the towering Christ-hymn: He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature—not a creature Himself but the heir and Lord over all creation. By Him were all things created, in heaven and in earth, visible and invisible, thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers; all things were created by Him and for Him. He is before all things, and by Him all things consist, holding the very universe together. He is the head of the body, the church, the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things He might have the preeminence. For it pleased the Father that in Him all fulness should dwell, and by Him to reconcile all things, having made peace through the blood of His cross. The dictionary reads Colossians 1 as the answer to every philosophy and every age that would make Christ less than He is: He is Creator, Sustainer, Head, and Reconciler, and in all things He must have the preeminence.
webster_summary: The first chapter of Colossians; the great hymn to Christ—image of the invisible God, Creator and Sustainer of all things, Head of the church, who in all things has the preeminence.

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
Col 1:17

Col 1:18

corruption_summary: The Arians and their heirs read “firstborn of every creature” to make Christ a creature; the chapter itself makes Him the Creator of all things and the heir over all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The ancient corruption the chapter has long been forced to answer is the Arian reading—revived by the Jehovah’s Witnesses and others—that takes “the firstborn of every creature” to mean Christ is the first and highest created being. But the very next verse forbids it: by Him were all things created; the Creator of all is not Himself among the created. “Firstborn” here is the title of the heir and Lord, the One who holds the rights of preeminence over all, not the first in a series of creatures. He is before all things, and by Him all things consist—language no creature could bear.

The principle to recover is the unqualified supremacy of Christ over creation, the church, and salvation. He is the image of the invisible God, Creator and Sustainer, Head of the body, the firstborn from the dead, the Reconciler who made peace by the blood of His cross. The Colossian heresy, like every age’s philosophy, sought to set something above or beside Him; the chapter answers that in all things—all things without exception—He must have the preeminence.

etymology: The fourteenth chapter of Isaiah; the taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon, with its “Lucifer, son of the morning.”
biblical_def: Isaiah 14 is the prophet’s taunt-song over the fall of the king of Babylon, the proud oppressor brought down to the grave, and one of the most searching passages in Scripture on the ruin that pride works. The LORD promises rest to His people from their bondage, and then puts in their mouth a proverb against the tyrant: How hath the oppressor ceased! The whole earth is at rest, and the very trees of the forest rejoice that no feller is come up against them. Hell from beneath is moved to meet him; the kings of the nations rise from their thrones to greet the once-mighty king now made weak as they. Then comes the famous cry: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! For he had said in his heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will be like the most High—the five great “I wills” of pride—yet he is brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit. The dictionary reads the chapter first of the historical king of Babylon, the proud tyrant judged by God; and, as the church has long discerned in the language of a creature reaching to be like the most High, an apt picture of the pride of Satan and the sure ruin of all who exalt themselves against God.
webster_summary: The fourteenth chapter of Isaiah; the taunt over the fallen king of Babylon—the five “I wills” of pride and the ruin of the oppressor brought down to the pit.

corruption_summary: Modern critics flatten the chapter to mere ancient political rhetoric and deny any reference beyond the human king; the church reads it of the Babylonian tyrant and discerns in it the pride and ruin of Satan.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the chapter’s reference. Its first and plain sense is the historical king of Babylon, the proud oppressor of God’s people, judged and brought down to the grave; modern critical readers who allow only this human reference are right as far as they go but wrong to forbid more. The church has long discerned, in the language of a being who would ascend above the stars of God and be like the most High and is cast down to the pit, an apt picture of the pride of Satan—the creature’s reach to usurp the Creator’s throne. The dictionary holds both: the Babylonian tyrant in the foreground, and behind him the ancient pride that fell from heaven.

The principle to recover is the certain ruin of pride that exalts itself against God. The five “I wills” of the chapter are the very grammar of rebellion—I will ascend, I will exalt, I will be like the most High—and they end in the sides of the pit. Whether in Babylon’s king, in the fallen accuser, or in the proud heart of any man, the lesson is one: God resists the proud, and everyone that exalteth himself shall be abased.

etymology: The first chapter of Paul’s first epistle to the Corinthians; the rebuke of divisions and the preaching of the cross as the wisdom of God.
biblical_def: First Corinthians 1 confronts a church torn by divisions and intoxicated with worldly wisdom, and answers both by exalting the cross of Christ. Paul beseeches the Corinthians, who were saying I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas, that they all speak the same thing and be perfectly joined together in the same mind, for Christ is not divided, and Paul was not crucified for them. He then sets the preaching of the cross against the wisdom of the world: the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness, but to them that are saved it is the power of God. God has made foolish the wisdom of this world; the Jews require a sign and the Greeks seek after wisdom, but Paul preaches Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumblingblock and to the Greeks foolishness, yet to them that are called the power of God and the wisdom of God. And God has chosen the foolish, weak, and base things of the world to confound the wise and mighty, that no flesh should glory in His presence—for of Him are the saved in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto them wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. The dictionary reads the chapter as the great rebuke of party spirit and human pride, and the enthroning of the crucified Christ as the only wisdom and power of God unto salvation.
webster_summary: The first chapter of 1 Corinthians; the rebuke of divisions and the preaching of Christ crucified as the power and wisdom of God against the wisdom of the world.

corruption_summary: The age that prizes worldly wisdom and party loyalty stumbles at the cross; the chapter answers that Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God, and no flesh may glory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption the chapter rebukes is perennial: the party spirit that names itself after men—I am of Paul, I of Apollos—and the worldly wisdom that finds the cross foolish. Every age that prizes eloquence, cleverness, and the approval of the wise repeats the Greek error of seeking after wisdom and stumbling at a crucified Saviour; every age that gathers around personalities rather than Christ repeats the Corinthian divisions. The remedy is not a more impressive wisdom but the offence of the cross preached plainly.

The principle to recover is the centrality and sufficiency of Christ crucified. The preaching of the cross is the power of God to them that are saved; God has chosen the foolish and weak things to confound the wise and mighty, that no flesh should glory in His presence but that he who glories should glory in the Lord. Christ is made unto His people wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption—the whole of salvation in Him—so that the church’s unity is found not in a favored teacher but in the one Lord who was crucified for her.

etymology: The twenty-first and final chapter of the Gospel of John; the risen Christ at the sea of Tiberias and the restoration of Peter.
biblical_def: John 21 is the closing chapter of the fourth Gospel, the risen Lord’s appearing to His disciples at the sea of Tiberias, the miraculous draught of fishes, and above all the tender restoration of Simon Peter. The disciples, having toiled all night and caught nothing, are told by the stranger on the shore to cast the net on the right side; the net is filled with a hundred fifty and three great fishes, and John knows that it is the Lord. After they have dined, the Lord turns to Peter, who had thrice denied Him, and asks three times, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?—one searching question for each denial. Three times Peter affirms his love, grieved that he is asked the third time, and three times the Lord commissions him: Feed my lambs; feed my sheep; feed my sheep. The thrice-denying disciple is thrice restored and charged to shepherd the flock. The Lord then foretells the death by which Peter would glorify God and bids him simply, Follow me. When Peter asks about John, the Lord answers, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. The Gospel closes confessing that the world itself could not contain the books of all that Jesus did. The dictionary reads John 21 as the gospel of restoring grace: the fallen disciple recommissioned by the love of Christ and sent to feed the sheep.
webster_summary: The final chapter of John; the risen Christ at the sea of Tiberias, the great catch, and the threefold restoration of Peter—“Lovest thou me? Feed my sheep.”

scriptures: So when they had dined, Jesus saith to Simon Peter, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my lambs.

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.
Jesus saith unto him, If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.
And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written. Amen.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though Rome presses “feed my sheep” into a Petrine supremacy the text does not teach; rightly read, it is the restoration of a fallen disciple.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misreading to answer is the Roman use of “Feed my sheep” to establish a Petrine supremacy and the papal office—as though Christ here made Peter the prince over the apostles and the church. But the threefold charge answers Peter’s threefold denial; it is restoration, not coronation. Peter is recommissioned to the common pastoral work all elders share—to feed the flock of God—not exalted to a monarchy over his brethren, who elsewhere stand as fellow-foundations and to whom the same keys are given. The chapter humbles Peter; it does not enthrone him.

The principle to recover is the restoring grace of Christ toward fallen disciples and the shepherd’s charge that flows from love to Him. The Lord does not cast off the disciple who denied Him but draws out his love and sends him to feed the sheep; the qualification for ministry is love to Christ, and the work is to feed His flock. And to Peter’s curiosity about another the Lord gives the word every disciple needs: what is that to thee? follow thou me.

etymology: The opening eighteen verses of the Gospel of John (John 1:1–18); Johannine, pertaining to the apostle John; prologue, Greek prologos, a foreword.
biblical_def: The Johannine Prologue is the opening of the fourth Gospel, John 1:1–18, one of the loftiest passages in all Scripture, in which the apostle declares the eternal deity of the Word, His agency in creation, His incarnation, and His revelation of the Father. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God—eternal, personal, distinct from the Father yet Himself fully God. All things were made by Him, and without Him was not anything made that was made; the Word is the Creator, not a creature. In Him was life, and the life was the light of men; the light shines in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not. Then the great mystery: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. He came unto His own, and His own received Him not; but to as many as received Him, He gave power to become the sons of God. The Prologue closes by declaring that no man has seen God at any time, but the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has declared Him. The dictionary reads the Johannine Prologue as the bedrock of orthodox Christology: the eternal Word, true God and true man, the Creator made flesh to reveal the Father and bring grace and truth.

Joh 1:3

Joh 1:14

Joh 1:18

corruption_summary: The Arians and their heirs mistranslate “the Word was God” to make Christ “a god”; the grammar and the whole Prologue confess the Word as true and eternal God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to answer is the old Arian denial of the Word’s full deity, pressed today by the Jehovah’s Witnesses in their rendering “the Word was a god.” But the Greek will not bear it: the Word was with God (distinct in Person) and the Word was God (one in essence); and the Prologue at once adds that all things were made by Him—the Creator of all is no creature. To make the Word a lesser, created god is to overthrow the very gospel the Prologue announces, for only true God made flesh could declare the Father and bring grace and truth.

The principle to recover is the orthodox confession of the eternal Word made flesh. The Word is eternal—in the beginning was the Word; personal—the Word was with God; divine—the Word was God; the Creator—all things were made by Him; and incarnate—the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. This is the bedrock of Nicea and Chalcedon and of all sound Christology: true God and true man in one Person, the only begotten Son who has declared the unseen Father.

etymology: The parable-song of Isaiah 5:1–7, in which the LORD’s vineyard brings forth wild grapes.
biblical_def: The Song of the Vineyard is the parable-song of Isaiah 5:1–7, in which the prophet sings of his Wellbeloved’s vineyard—planted on a very fruitful hill, hedged, cleared of stones, planted with the choicest vine, furnished with a tower and a winepress—and yet, when the owner looked for grapes, it brought forth wild grapes. The LORD then asks the searching question: What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? Because it yielded only sour and worthless fruit, He will take away its hedge and break down its wall, and it shall be trodden down and laid waste, the rain withheld from it. Then the prophet unveils the song’s meaning: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah His pleasant plant; He looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. The chapter follows with the sixfold woe—woe to them that join house to house, that call evil good and good evil, that put darkness for light. The dictionary reads the Song of the Vineyard as God’s lament and indictment over a privileged people who returned His care with rotten fruit, and as the warning, fulfilled again in the parable of the wicked husbandmen, that where God has done all and the fruit is wanting, judgment follows.
webster_summary: The parable-song of Isaiah 5:1–7; the LORD’s well-tended vineyard, the house of Israel, brings forth wild grapes and is given to judgment.
webster_full: SONG OF THE VINEYARD, the parable-song of Isaiah 5:1–7.

It brings forth wild grapes despite all His care.
The vineyard is the house of Israel, the men of Judah His pleasant plant.
He looked for judgment and righteousness, but found oppression and a cry.

Isa 5:4

Isa 5:7

Isa 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the very age Isaiah indicts—calling evil good and good evil—is recognizable in the moral inversions of the present hour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle the song presses is the accountability of a privileged people for the fruit God seeks. Israel had every advantage—the hedge, the tower, the choicest vine—and returned wild grapes; and the LORD asks what more He could have done. The warning is not Israel’s alone: where God lavishes care—upon a nation, a church, a soul—and looks for the fruit of righteousness and finds oppression and a cry, judgment is just. The sixth woe of the chapter is strikingly modern: woe to them that call evil good and good evil, that put darkness for light—the very inversion of the present age.

The principle to recover is the fruit God requires of those He has favored. He looked for judgment and righteousness; the vine that yields only sour grapes despises the husbandry that planted it. The Lord Jesus took up the song in the parable of the wicked husbandmen and applied it to the leaders who would reject Him, warning that the kingdom would be given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof. God’s care lays an obligation; the well-tended vine must bring forth good grapes, or the hedge is taken away.

etymology: The post-exilic prophetic book of Zechariah; the Hebrew name Zekaryah, “the LORD remembers.”
biblical_def: The prophecy of Zechariah is the post-exilic book of the prophet who, with Haggai, stirred the returned remnant to rebuild the temple, and whose visions and oracles are among the most richly messianic in all the Old Testament. Zechariah opens with a call to repentance—turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts—and unfolds in a series of night visions of the LORD’s jealousy for Jerusalem, the cleansing of Joshua the high priest, and the promise of the Branch, the Servant who shall build the temple of the LORD and bear the glory. The later chapters pour out prophecies of the coming King and Shepherd that the Gospels record fulfilled in Christ: the King coming to Zion lowly and riding upon an ass; the thirty pieces of silver, the price at which the Shepherd was valued, cast to the potter; the LORD pierced, on whom they shall look and mourn; the Shepherd smitten and the sheep scattered. The book closes looking to the day when the LORD shall be king over all the earth, and holiness unto the LORD shall be written even upon the bells of the horses. The dictionary reads Zechariah as a fountain of messianic prophecy, the book that, more than almost any other, foretold the humble King, the pierced and smitten Shepherd, and the final reign of the LORD over all the earth.
webster_summary: The post-exilic prophecy of Zechariah; visions of the LORD’s jealousy for Jerusalem and a fountain of messianic prophecy—the humble King, the smitten Shepherd, the pierced LORD.
webster_full: ZECHARIAH, PROPHECY OF, the post-exilic prophet who urged the temple’s rebuilding.

Foretells the thirty pieces of silver, the pierced LORD, and the smitten Shepherd.
scriptures: Zec 9:9

Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.
And I said unto them, If ye think good, give me my price; and if not, forbear. So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.

And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
Zec 13:7

Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though critical readers deny the unity of the book and the predictive force of its messianic prophecies; the Gospels confess them fulfilled in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to answer is the critical denial that touches the book: the division of Zechariah into an authentic first part and a later “Deutero-Zechariah,” and the refusal of genuine predictive prophecy, so that the uncanny correspondences with the life of Christ are explained away as vague poetry or after-the-fact reading. The dictionary holds the unity and the predictive power of the book. The Gospels themselves cite these very texts as fulfilled: the King on the ass at the triumphal entry, the thirty pieces of silver cast to the potter, the pierced One looked upon, the smitten Shepherd and scattered sheep at Gethsemane. This is prophecy, not coincidence.

The principle to recover is the messianic unity of Scripture, with Zechariah a chief witness. The book that urged the rebuilding of the stone temple pointed beyond it to the Branch who would build the true temple and reign as King and Priest; its King comes lowly to Zion, is valued at a slave’s price, is pierced and smitten, and shall yet be king over all the earth. The LORD remembers—the meaning of the prophet’s name—and keeps every word concerning His Christ.
